strengths: Introduces a novel and conceptually elegant representation (FUSE) for maps between 3D shapes based on flow matching, using a shared Gaussian anchor distribution to bridge embedding spaces of a source and target shape, enabling zero-shot correspondence without pairwise optimization or large-scale training.

The representation is genuinely representation-agnostic: the paper demonstrates applicability across meshes, point clouds, SDFs, and volumetric (tetrahedral) meshes, as well as inter-representation matching, which is an advantage over pipelines tied to a specific discretization.

Strong experimental validation across four benchmarks (FAUST, SMAL, SHREC20, KINECT) against a wide range of axiomatic and learned baselines (KNN, OT, FMaps and variants, NDP, ZoomOut, NAM), with FUSE achieving competitive or superior accuracy and notably higher coverage due to its invertibility-by-construction property.

Thoughtful ablations: comparison of embedding strategies (xyz, WKS, geodesic, FMNet) showing the flow's distributional-alignment effect, and comparison against the closely related diffusion-based GeomDist approach (DDIM) showing FUSE's deterministic FM inversion yields lower divergence and better map accuracy.

Demonstrates versatility beyond pure matching, with applications to human scan fitting/skinning via SMPL-X, mesh parametrization/UV mapping, and volumetric correspondence, showing the representation can serve as a general-purpose backbone, and can be used to initialize existing refinement methods (FUSE+ZO, FUSE+NAM).

Clear articulation of the method's relation to prior work (Flow Matching, Geometry Distributions), with a reasoned discussion of why FM's exact bidirectionality is preferable to diffusion-based approximate inversion for this task.
weaknesses: The method relies on a task-tailored pointwise embedding (e.g., geodesic distances to landmarks) that must already be reasonably informative for the flow to help; the paper notes the flow does not help when embeddings are already well-aligned or are not alignable at all, suggesting dependence on the quality of an externally supplied feature embedding.

The maps produced lack smoothness compared to FMaps-based methods, attributed to the non-smooth nature of flow inversion from surface to distribution; refinement strategies (ZO, NAM) mitigate but do not fully resolve this, and the root cause is not deeply analyzed.

Point-cloud-only matching is explicitly reported as a weak setting due to unreliable geodesic distance estimation on unstructured data, narrowing the claimed representation-agnostic generality for the purely point-cloud case.

Landmark-based geodesic embeddings require manual/semantic landmark selection, and sensitivity to landmark count/noise or fully automatic selection is not extensively analyzed, which somewhat limits insight into the robustness of the claimed zero-shot generality.

Some sections (e.g., SDF benchmark discussion, scan fitting, parametrization) are only qualitatively or partially quantitatively evaluated in the main paper, with deeper analysis deferred to supplementary material.
Computational cost/training time comparisons against baselines are not clearly reported despite the paper's claim of computational efficiency.
